title: The emperor's notebook
hook: Marcus wrote in Greek, to himself, often on campaign, and the title "Meditations" came later

segments.voice: Yesterday, the week closed with Rumi as he was: a Muslim, a scholar, a Sufi. Your line was a love he thought was wide.

Somebody opens your notes app. Not your posts, your notes. The reminders to yourself. Be patient with Dad. Stop checking your phone. You're not as tired as you think. A little embarrassing, and also a truer picture of you than any post. The emperor of Rome kept notes like that: reminders to himself, in Greek, some of them, it seems, written far from Rome on the Danube frontier, around the year 170. As far as anyone can tell, they were meant for no one else. Today, the emperor's notebook.
screen: `YOUR NOTES APP, NOT YOUR POSTS.` → `A TENT ON THE DANUBE, AROUND 170.` → `THE EMPEROR'S NOTEBOOK.`

segments.voice: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from 161 to 180. He spent much of his last decade at war along the Danube frontier, and it's likely that much of his notebook was written there, in camp. A few headings in the manuscripts seem to place him: one book ends with a note that it was written among the Quadi, a people on the far side of the river, and another reads: at Carnuntum, a Roman fort. Three things are worth knowing. First, he wrote in Greek, not Latin. Greek was the language of philosophy, and Marcus had studied the Stoics, among them the former slave Epictetus. Second, he wrote to himself. The notes scold, remind, encourage and repeat, the way you do when you haven't learned something yet. That's part of why they feel so alive: this isn't a man who has arrived; it's a man practicing. Third, the famous title isn't his. The old manuscripts carry a Greek heading usually translated to himself, and it may have been added by whoever copied the notes after his death. Meditations is what English readers later called the book. It survived by a thin thread of copies and was first printed in the 1550s. So beside Rumi this camp, remember the difference. Rumi spoke his book aloud to a friend who wrote it down. Marcus wrote his alone, for no one. Both, somehow, made it through the centuries.
screen: `WRITTEN ON CAMPAIGN, BY THE DANUBE.` · `IN GREEK, THE LANGUAGE OF PHILOSOPHY.` · `NOTES THAT SCOLD AND REPEAT.` · `THE TITLE CAME LATER.` · then, large: `TO HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Ask what you keep needing to remember and keep forgetting: be kinder to your sister, rest is not failure, finish before you start the next thing. Find one plain, honest sentence, the way you'd say it to a friend, and say it inside, slowly. If you can, write it down somewhere you'll see it again.
Carnuntum, the Roman fort on the Danube where part of Marcus Aurelius's private notebook was likely written. Today's word.
Your line: to himself. Even an emperor needed reminding, again and again. Day one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often keep it by the bed and read a single short section at a time, and many who follow modern Stoic practice keep their own journal of notes to themselves.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens 'Imagine ... Now picture' and no longer repeats day 157's lamplit-tent scene; cut 'the most powerful man in the world'; 'never meant anyone to read them' hedged (as day 157 was); the Carnuntum note no longer asserts it begins a book (placement varies by edition); 'especially Epictetus since his youth' overstated Meditations 1.7, now 'among them Epictetus'.
Headings: book 1 ends 'among the Quadi at the Granua'; book 2 begins 'at Carnuntum'. Whether these are Marcus's own is debated. Confirm.
First printed edition: Xylander, Zurich, 1558/1559; script says 'the 1550s'. Confirm.
The Greek title ta eis heauton may be a later addition; stated with 'may'. Confirm.
Epictetus's influence (via the Discourses, which Marcus says Rusticus lent him, Meditations 1.7): confirm 'since his youth' is not overstated.
Dating: much written in the 170s; 'around the year 170' used for the scene. Confirm.
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
